glossary.meaning: Conscience is the inner court where our whole teaching plays out. Under God's Law, it feels terror. Under God's promise, it finds comfort. It is not a guide that tells us right from wrong. It is a court that stands accused, then is set free.
glossary.world_word: conscience -- 'terrified,' 'anxious,' 'captive'; the court where our doctrine is decided

glossary.meaning: Faith is trust that holds onto God's own promise. It is not simply believing a story is true. This trust alone makes us right with God, apart from our works. But faith never stands on nothing. It rests on the Word and the sacraments.
glossary.world_word: faith -- trust that clings to God's promise, 'faith alone'

glossary.meaning: The household is where our catechism was taught. Our books told a father to question his family and servants at least once a week. He was to lead them in prayer morning, evening, and at meals. That is how ordinary people were meant to learn the faith.
glossary.world_word: the household -- father, wife, children, servants; the catechism's own site

glossary.meaning: God rules us two ways. Through the Word, he rules the spiritual kingdom, and makes us Christians. Through the sword, he rules the civil kingdom, and restrains evil. We keep both, and confuse neither with the other.
glossary.world_word: the two governments -- God's spiritual rule by the Word, and secular rule by the sword

glossary.meaning: Baptism makes every one of us a priest. There is no rank among us, only different tasks. A father is a priest in his own home. Still, no one may preach in public without being properly called.
glossary.world_word: 'we are all priests' -- consecrated in baptism, no estate difference, only office

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: the Small Catechism's Second Article -- the creed and its explanation, said by the household itself, in its own first person, as 'I believe'
pull_quotes.text:
And in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord. He was conceived by the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary. He suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died and was buried. He descended to Hell. On the third day he rose again from the dead. He ascended to Heaven and sat down at the right hand of God the Almighty Father. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.
What does this mean?
I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord! He redeemed me, a lost and condemned person. He bought me and won me from all sins, from death and from the authority of the Devil. It did not cost him gold or silver, but his holy, precious blood, his innocent body -- his death! Because of this, I am his very own. I will live under him in his kingdom. I will serve him in righteousness, innocence and blessedness forever, just as he is risen from death, lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: the Augsburg Confession, Article VII -- signed at the 1530 Diet of Augsburg by an Elector, princes, and two city councils who confessed it, not one preacher's own private teaching
pull_quotes.text:
They also teach that one holy Church will go on forever. The Church is the community of saints, in which the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments are rightly given.
For the true unity of the Church, it is enough to agree on the Gospel's teaching and on how the sacraments are given. Nor do human traditions -- that is, rites or ceremonies set up by people -- need to be alike everywhere. As Paul says: one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, and so on.

pull_quotes.speaker_or_author: the Large Catechism, the Seventh Commandment's own household explanation
pull_quotes.text: But beware of this. The poor man may come to you, and there are so many now. He must buy with the penny of his daily wages and live on it. You may be harsh to him, as though everyone lived by your favor. You may skin and scrape to the bone. Besides that, with pride and haughtiness, you may turn away the man you ought to give to for nothing. Then he will go away wretched and sorrowful. He can complain to no one, so he will cry and call to heaven. Then beware, I say again, as of the devil himself. For such groaning and calling will be no joke. It will have a weight that will prove too heavy for you and all the world. For it will reach Him who takes care of the poor, sorrowful hearts. He will not allow them to go unavenged.

cite.text:
The sinner is 'freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith' (AC IV, 234-239). Works and merit are refused as the ground: 'faith alone, without works, justifies, makes free and saves' (Treatise on Christian Liberty, v2 11780-11781); 'the promises of God give what the commands of God ask... He alone commands. He also alone fulfils' (v2 11817-11820).
Its first, limited form is the target of the 1517 disputation: 'The true treasure of the Church is the Most Holy Gospel of the glory and the grace of God' (Th. 62). That thesis answers the claim that giving to the poor is 'a better work than buying pardons' (Th. 43).
The doctrine runs through seven streams of evidence, in both of this world's voices: disputation, treatise, sermon, catechism teaching, and hymn, along with the sustained argument of The Bondage of the Will and Melanchthon's confession. That confession calls it 'the chief topic of Christian doctrine' (Ap IV, 561-562).
It recurs across all seven streams, and other gravities say in their own texts that they depend on it. Promise and sign approaches the sacrament "with faith alone," and the terrified and comforted conscience refers the whole doctrine to the conscience (AC 552-553). Estate, office, and calling redefines works by faith, while vows, chastity, and marriage refuses vows as merit.
It shapes people as a doctrine prescribed and preached, and it is the one gravity the founder says his own congregation already held, in 1522: 'you are more learned herein than I' (v2 14665-14666). That any wider congregation held it rests only on thin inference, so what the founder prescribed is kept apart from what congregations received.
Much of the movement's shape follows from it, including the target of the 1517 protest and the structure of the 1520 treatises. It also explains why the catechism puts the Creed over the Commandments, and why the Confession's own order sets Article IV before Article V.
It persists from 1517 to 1531 in every kind of writing, but by the 1540s it thins to hymn and Table Talk only.
It reinforces the Word, promise and sign, and the household catechism, as well as the conscience, "must" and "free", vows and marriage, and embattled Christendom. Its reinforcement of the bodily presence and German for the people is only thin. It reshapes the two governments and estate, office, and calling, and it competes with only one: hearers and repeaters of words.
The doctrine is well documented, and within this world's own writings the case for it is strong on every count. The confession's own voice calls it "the chief topic," and the evidence fully bears that organizing weight rather than falling short of it.
It appears in both of this world's voices, across six kinds of writing. There is also one thin trace from a household: Katharina von Bora (TT 3147-3148), who speaks of coldness in prayer, not of faith itself. As for how it was received, the founder says it was received, in Wittenberg only, in 1522.
It arose from the friar's founding conviction and from the laity's need for assurance. The papal bull and the Leipzig dispute then turned an argument into the movement's identity, and that papal pressure, in its early and its ongoing form, held and intensified it.
The imperial force intensified it again into a confessional definition at Augsburg: Article IV of the Augsburg Confession in 1530, and the Apology's "chief topic" in 1531.
Then the reform's own "new spirits", the internal radical force, used the formula for a purpose it was not built for. The doctrine was fenced again rather than broken, and by 1529 the Large Catechism answers that faith 'must have something which it believes... upon which it stands and rests' (LC 3916-3921).
After 1531 it is carried only in hymn and Table Talk, a stage that lies at the edge of the world's time window, outside the formal forces mapping.

In the confessional voice's own doctrine of justification, "accounted righteous" (imputed, forensic) names the term's real and controlling sense, and "the making of a righteous man out of an unrighteous" is the same single act described a second, looser way - not an independent claim standing beside the first, but a paraphrase of it, subordinate to it.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: Did you believe people are saved by faith alone, not works?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: Yes, but hear what we meant by both words before you judge the claim. Faith was not simply believing a story is true. It was trust that clings to a promise spoken from outside us, conceived from hearing the Word and not produced by our own effort, and it never stood on nothing, since it rested on the Word and the sacraments. Our confession, signed before the emperor, said this trust alone is why a sinner is freely counted right with God for Christ's sake, and not by our own strength, merit, or work. We were accused of teaching that works do not matter, and we answered that good works are necessary, not to earn grace but because God commands them. Good works were not only prayer, fasting, and almsgiving, which names them too narrowly. They were the ordinary things a person does in faith: working, walking, eating, sleeping. None of it was good without faith, and all of it was good in faith, commanded and never a price. The Apology that defended our confession even states this two ways in one paragraph. A person is reckoned righteous, and a person is made righteous out of an unrighteous one. It does not say which wording rules the other, and we do not settle that for you either.

cite.text:
The three parts every Christian must know are to be taught by the father, examined weekly, and sung and prayed morning and evening. 'the ordinary Christian, who cannot read the Scriptures, is required to learn and know the Ten Commandments, the Creed, and the Lord's Prayer... these three contain fully and completely everything that is in the Scriptures' (v2 13182-13186). 'it is the duty of every father of a family to question and examine his children and servants at least once a week' (LC 241-243). 'The Simple Way a Father Should Present Them to His Household' (SC 45).
This gravity is deliberately limited: it is a claim about the program, and it never claims that any household actually held to it.
The program recurs widely, appearing in catechism teaching, in sermons by implication, in a hymnal preface, and in conversation. It also appears in the confession and the Apology and in one participant's witness, and other gravities depend on it broadly.
Its shaping power splits in two, and that split is the central tension in how this gravity is judged. As a prescribed program it holds fully. It is the most fully specified way of forming people in the whole library, reaching down to reciting at mealtimes and to food withheld until the lessons are repeated (LC 333-336). As formation actually achieved, it rests only on thin inference, because no visitation record, parish register, or lay witness confirms that any household did it.
Its explanatory reach is broad, and it persists across kinds of writing from 1520 to 1543. Across regions, though, it fails, since nothing shows any household or parish outside Wittenberg, so its persistence holds only in part.
It reinforces nearly every other gravity: justified by faith alone, the Word, promise and sign, and the terrified and comforted conscience. It also reinforces the two governments; estate, office, and calling; vows, chastity, and marriage; German for the people; and embattled Christendom. Its support for the bodily presence is only thin. It reshapes "must" and "free", and it competes with only one: hearers and repeaters of words.
The written prescriptions are well documented, and Walter's witness is widely accepted. Any household's actual practice rests only on thin inference. Scholars contest how reception should even be read, in the debate that follows Strauss.
This record covers the program as defined above, where the evidence is well attested: the bulk of the 1529 writings, plus the two confessional texts. Read more broadly, to include reception as well as the program, the evidence would place it lower. This record states that alternative openly rather than hiding it.
This is the highest-stakes case in this world where how strongly a pattern organizes it and how well that is evidenced pull apart. As a program, it organizes at the highest level this account recognizes, and the program is well attested, but the evidence for how it was received is thin. That thinness is not smoothed over; it is named as sitting outside what this record actually claims.
The program appears in all four kinds of writing and voice, but the mechanism of the father in the household is Luther's alone. Evidence of how it was received is absent, the largest single gap of this kind in this world.
It arose in response to a question: what would replace indulgence, confession, and sacrament as the way lay people were formed? That question itself arose from the laity's need for assurance. Between 1520 and 1529 its audience shifted from "the ordinary Christian, who cannot read" to the negligent pastor and the father of the household. That shift came from the territorial church's own need to inspect.
The state of the parishes, as the founder reported it, intensified it. By its own account, the Large Catechism preface exists because pastors are negligent. Because it is the printed object in the household, print as a medium carried it. It was held within the confessional writings and entered the Book of Concord in 1580 by reference. That links it to the confessional-territorial change and to transmission at the edge of the window. It also carries the household's own daily prayer for the prince, which ties it to the imperial frame.

Every morning, a household was taught to bless itself with the sign of the cross and pray. Every week, the father was told to question his children and servants on the catechism. The Large Catechism says children are to be given neither food nor drink until they can repeat the parts.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: How did a person actually become one of you? Walk me through it.

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: A person became one of us the way a child did: examined, not simply told. Every household was to teach its own the three parts. The commandments came first, then the creed, then the Lord's Prayer. Mornings began with the sign of the cross and a short prayer against the evil enemy. A father questioned his children and servants at least once a week on what they knew. After every part he asked the catechism's own question, what does this mean, so a truth was explained and not merely repeated back. Confession had two parts too: admitting sin, then hearing forgiveness spoken as though from God himself. We treasured it. We never forced it, and we never demanded a full list of every sin. None of this was owed to a person, or earned by them. It was the promise, carried to the ears where it could be heard. We can tell you the whole shape of that program, down to the hour. We cannot tell you whether any one household walked through it exactly this way. No diary, no visitation report, and no letter from inside a Saxon home survives in our record. What survives is the program every household was told to follow. That is the program we have just walked you through, and not any one person's path through it.

cite.text: At his table, Luther told his students that his whole life was patience. He needed it with the Pope, with heretics, with servants, and "with Kate my wife." In another talk, Katharina von Bora is remembered asking why the old church prayed so hard while their own household prayed cold and careless.

exchange.speaker: participant
exchange.text: What was life like for the women among you — in their own words, where your record has them?

exchange.speaker: representative
exchange.text: One sentence. That is the whole of what we hold in a woman's own words, anywhere in our record. It was asked at our founder's own table, remembered years later by a student who set it down: why, she wanted to know, did the old church pray so often and with such vehemence, while our own household prayed cold and careless? Her name was Katharina von Bora, our founder's own wife - and that question, passed through several hands before it reached us, is the one place in this whole record where a woman speaks in her own voice at all. Beyond it: nothing. No letter of her own, no second conversation, nothing about her own daily life, her own convictions, or her own formation survives anywhere we hold. We will not build more around that one sentence than it can bear. If you want the women among us in their own words, this is the whole of what our record has to give you - one question, about coldness in prayer, asked once, remembered by someone else.

quiet.statement:
Where is our own record thinnest? On what any actual household or parish did with what it was given. We can tell you exactly what a household was to do -- morning, table, and night. We can tell you exactly what a father was to ask his children and servants each week. That program is the most fully specified thing we hold, down to the hour. Whether it was kept is a different matter. The church in Saxony inspected its own parishes, starting in 1527, and wrote down what it found. Those reports exist. We do not hold them. What we hold instead is our founder's own testimony, given more than once, that common people held the Gospel too lightly, and that some pastors were negligent. That testimony is real. It is his own, said plainly and said more than once. But it is not, on its own, a report from any actual parish. We do not let it stand as one.
Two other places are just as thin. Our fellowship broke plainly with the cities who read the Supper differently. We can state our own position: Christ is truly present, in and under the bread and wine. But the argument itself, and what it felt like from our own side, has not come down to us. No text we hold names Zwingli or the meeting at Marburg. Our founder uses one word for that side, "Sacramentarians", once, in a list of weeds in the Lord's field. And no woman among us left her own word. There is one question, about coldness in prayer, asked at our founder's own table -- but even that was remembered by someone else, not written by her.
That is where we are thinnest: what real people made of what they were told to believe and do. For that we have only our founder's own testimony about them.

who_speaks.text: Six figures anchor this world's voice, each only as far as the record reaches. Luther began the reform in 1517 and is held in his own letters, sermons, and catechisms. Melanchthon drafted the Augsburg Confession of 1530. Katharina von Bora is held in one remembered question about prayer. Johann Walter remembered the first German Mass. Paul Speratus is known as the author of three hymns in the first hymn-book. John and Henry, two young monks, were burned at Brussels in 1523 and are known by their first names alone.

documented_stories.teaser: A friar wrote to the archbishop in whose name indulgences were being preached. He asked for correction and sent ninety-five statements for debate.
documented_stories.tellable_as: A friar at Wittenberg writes to Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz in the most respectful terms he can find. The indulgence preachers work under the Archbishop's name. The friar warns that people are being taught false beliefs, and he sends ninety-five statements for open debate.
documented_stories.telling:
On the last day of October, 1517, Martin Luther sat down to write to a man far above him. Luther was an Augustinian friar who taught theology at Wittenberg. Albrecht was Archbishop of Magdeburg and Mainz, and Primate of the Church.

Luther greeted the Archbishop as "Most Reverend Father in Christ and Most Illustrious Prince." He called himself "the dregs of humanity," amazed at his own boldness in writing.

Indulgences for the building of St. Peter's in Rome were being preached under Albrecht's name. Luther said he had not heard the preaching himself, and he grieved over what its hearers now believed. They thought a bought letter of indulgence made their salvation sure. They thought souls flew out of purgatory as soon as a gift went into the money-box. "O God, most good!" he wrote. "Thus souls committed to your care, good Father, are taught to their death."

He asked the Archbishop to withdraw the instruction the preachers followed. Otherwise someone else might do it in public, to the Archbishop's own shame. He signed himself "Brother Martin Luther," and added one line more. If it pleased him, the Archbishop might look over "these my Disputations." They were ninety-five statements for university debate, sent along with the letter.
documented_stories.title: A Letter to an Archbishop

documented_stories.teaser: Luther told his students he knelt before Cardinal Cajetan. He would not say the one word asked of him, Revoco, "I recant."
documented_stories.tellable_as: Summoned to Augsburg in 1518, Luther is told by an Italian that one word will do: "Revoco," I recant. He goes to Cardinal Cajetan, kneels, and then lies flat on the ground. The next day the Cardinal asks where he can hope to find safety. Luther answers, "Under Heaven."
documented_stories.telling:
In the summer of 1518 Luther was summoned to Augsburg, as he told his students years later at his own table. Frederick, the Elector of Saxony, gave him a strong escort and a safe-conduct. He was warned not to trust the Italians.

He waited three days for the Emperor's own safe-conduct. In that time an Italian led him to Cardinal Cajetan, urging him the whole way to say one word, Revoco, which means I recant. Say it, the man promised, and the Cardinal would send him home to his Elector in honor.

Before the Cardinal, Luther said, he knelt on his knees and then went all the way down to the ground. He stayed there until Cajetan three times told him to rise. The Cardinal was pleased, and he hoped, Luther said, that Luther would think better of things.

The next day Luther came again and would not recant anything. In Luther's memory, the Cardinal asked whether he thought the Pope cared for Germany, or that princes would raise armies to defend him. "Oh, no; where wilt thou remain in safety?" Cajetan asked.

"Under Heaven," Luther answered.
documented_stories.title: Kneeling Before a Cardinal
documented_stories.when: Summer 1518, Augsburg, as Luther told it later at his table

documented_stories.teaser: Luther told his students he went to Worms despite warnings. He said he would accept correction in everything except what touches Scripture.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Warned on the road that he is already condemned at Worms, Luther answers that he will go anyway, "although in Worms there were as many devils as there are tiles on the houses." Warned again that he may be burned, he goes on. Before the Emperor and the assembled Empire he says he cannot give up his books of doctrine. The next day, before the Bishops, he says he will accept instruction in everything except what touches the Holy Scriptures.
documented_stories.telling:
At Erfurt, on the road to Worms, a herald asked Luther whether he still meant to go on. Word had spread that he was condemned.

So Luther told it, years later, to the students at his table. He had been summoned to the Diet under an imperial safe-conduct, and within a day of his leaving it was broken. His books were burned at Worms before he arrived. He answered the herald that he would go, "although in Worms there were as many devils as there are tiles on the houses."

Before the Emperor and Electors, Dr. Eck asked whether the books on the table were his. "Yea, they are mine," he answered. Some were books of doctrine, and those he could not recant. He asked for time to consider, and was given one day and one night.

The next day the Bishops pressed him. "God's Word is not my word," he told them, "therefore I know not how to give it away." In whatever did not touch the Holy Scriptures, he would obey.

Word reached the Emperor, wrongly, that he had recanted. A Bishop came to ask if he had left his cause to the Emperor. He had not, Luther said, and never meant to.
documented_stories.title: Luther Before the Emperor
documented_stories.when: 1521, Worms, as Luther told it years later at his table

documented_stories.teaser: Luther came back from hiding against his prince's instruction. He found Wittenberg in disorder and told his congregation he saw no signs of love among them.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Against his prince's wishes, Luther leaves the Wartburg and returns to a Wittenberg in disorder. He preaches eight days running and tells his congregation to their faces that they have learned the words of the reform but not yet its love.
documented_stories.telling:
In March of 1522, Luther left the Wartburg, where he had been hidden since Worms. The Elector had told him to stay, and he came back to Wittenberg anyway.

While he was away, the reform had run ahead of him under his colleague Karlstadt and others. The town had fallen into disorder over how fast the old forms of worship should be swept away.

Luther preached eight days running. A witness named Kessler was there, and he said Luther first explained the day's Gospel. Then he "dropped the text and took up the present affair."

"And here, dear friends," Luther said, "have you not grievously failed? I see no signs of love among you." They had learned the doctrine, he told them plainly, without living it. "Let us beware lest Wittenberg become Capernaum."

The kingdom of God, he said, lies in deeds and works. "God does not want hearers and repeaters of words, but doers and followers who exercise themselves in the faith that worketh by love." A faith without love, he told them, was no faith at all. It was "a counterfeit of faith."
documented_stories.title: Eight Days of Preaching

documented_stories.teaser: Two young monks, John and Henry, refused to give up their teaching and were burned. Luther wrote a ballad about them within the year.
documented_stories.tellable_as: In July of 1523, two young monks named John and Henry were burned at Brussels for refusing to take back what they had come to believe. Within months, Luther wrote a ballad about them in Wittenberg.
documented_stories.telling:
Luther's ballad opens by calling itself "a new and wondrous story," sung "to his great praise and glory," the glory of God.

On the first of July, 1523, two young monks named John and Henry were burned at Brussels. Theologians from Louvain had examined them and pressed them to give up the evangelical teaching, and they refused. Word reached Wittenberg quickly, and within months Luther had written his song.

It calls them "two youths, highly gifted with rich and heavenly graces." In the song, the Louvain theologians try every device to make them recant, and the two stand firm "like rocks." In its words, "for God's dear Word they shed their blood," and "they won the crown of martyrs."

The ballad says their monks' habits were stripped from them before the burning. They answered, it says, with "a cheerful Amen," glad to be free of "Satan's mock and masquerade."
documented_stories.title: Two Young Monks Burned at Brussels

documented_stories.teaser: A tradition says a wanderer from Prussia once sang a hymn under Luther's window. The hymn was by Paul Speratus, and the song moved Luther.
documented_stories.tellable_as: In Wittenberg, a wanderer down from Prussia is remembered to have sung Paul Speratus's own hymn, "Es ist das Heil uns kommen her," beneath Luther's window. The tradition says it moved him deeply. We have no word of when it happened. We do not know who the singer was. We cannot say the scene ever happened at all.
documented_stories.telling:
Wittenberg's first hymn-book was printed in 1524, and it held eight hymns. Four of them were Luther's own, and three were by Paul Speratus. One of those three was "Es ist das Heil uns kommen her."

Bacon notes that in that same book, the 1524 "Eight Songs," Luther's three versions of Psalms are all set to this hymn's tune.

Bacon's Introduction relates a tradition about the hymn. An unnamed wanderer came down from Prussia, the tradition says. He stood beneath Luther's window and sang Speratus's hymn, and the singing moved Luther deeply.
documented_stories.title: A Hymn Under Luther's Window
documented_stories.when: Undated, tied to the first Wittenberg hymn-book of 1524

documented_stories.teaser: Johann Walter wrote in old age that Luther kept him three weeks at Wittenberg. Luther worked out there how to sing the Gospel and Epistle in German.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Years later, Johann Walter, who made music with Luther, recalled three weeks at Wittenberg. Luther was setting the Gospel and Epistle to music. Walter also recalled the charity-scholars who went from door to door for bread, and the day the first German Mass was sung.
documented_stories.telling:
Walter remembered Luther choosing the Sixth Tone for the Gospel. "Our Lord Christ is a good Friend," Luther said, "and his words are full of love," and so he chose it.

Johann Walter, Luther's partner in music, set down those words in his old age, some forty years later.

Luther had written to the Elector of Saxony and to Duke Johannsen, Walter recalled. He asked them to send Walter and the old musician Conrad Rupff to Wittenberg. They were to help decide how the church's tones should be set. Luther chose the Eighth Tone for the Epistle.

He set the notes himself over the Epistles, the Gospels and the Words of Institution. Then he sang them over for Walter's judgment. He "kept me three weeks long at Wittenberg," Walter wrote, to write out the notes over some of the Gospels and Epistles, "until the first German Mass was sung in the parish church."

Walter had to stay and hear it. Then he was to carry a copy of the Mass to the Elector at Torgau, from Doctor Luther.
documented_stories.title: Three Weeks Setting the Mass in German
documented_stories.when: Mid-1520s, Wittenberg, as Johann Walter remembered it

documented_stories.teaser: A father was to question his children and servants every week. The young were to get no food or drink until they could say the parts.
documented_stories.tellable_as: Every morning, a household was taught to bless itself with the sign of the cross and pray. Every week, the father was told to question his children and servants on the catechism. The Large Catechism says children are to be given neither food nor drink until they can repeat the parts.
documented_stories.telling:
The two catechisms set out a program for every household, in detail. No source names a single household that kept it.

Mornings were to begin with the sign of the cross and a short prayer. It asked that "the evil enemy will not gain power over me." Afterward one might "go about your work and perhaps sing a song inspired by the Ten Commandments." A father was to teach the Commandments in what the Small Catechism calls "the simple way," one at a time.

The Small Catechism gave a servant words for confession. The servant was to say he had "served my master unfaithfully." The master or lady of the house was given words too, confessing they had "not faithfully led my children, servants or wife to God's glory."

The Large Catechism's preface made the weekly duty plain. A father was "to question and examine his children and servants at least once a week." The youngest were to learn the parts "word for word" and recite them each day. The preface says that "until they repeat them, they should be given neither food nor drink."

A head of the house was to hold his servants to the same standard. He was "not to keep them in his house if they do not know these things and are unwilling to learn them."
documented_stories.title: What a Household Was Told to Do

documented_stories.teaser: Melanchthon wrote the movement's confession for the Diet, and an elector, princes and two city councils signed it. Luther's name is not among them.
documented_stories.tellable_as: In 1530 at Augsburg, a statement of faith written by Melanchthon goes to the Emperor. An elector, princes and two city councils sign it. They call themselves his "faithful subjects."
documented_stories.telling:
"Most Invincible Emperor, Caesar Augustus, Most Clement Lord." With that greeting opens the confession Melanchthon wrote for the Diet at Augsburg in 1530.

The Emperor had called the Diet to deal with "measures against the Turk," the ancient enemy of the Christian name. It was also to hear the quarrels over religion in the German lands.

At the close of the confession stands a list of names. It begins with John, Duke of Saxony and Elector. George, Margrave of Brandenburg, follows, then Ernest, Duke of Lueneburg. Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, is there, with John Frederick, Duke of Saxony, and Francis, Duke of Lueneburg. Wolfgang, Prince of Anhalt, is named next. Two city councils close the list, the Senate and Magistracy of Nuremberg and the Senate of Reutlingen. Luther's name is not among them.

Princes and city councils stand together and call themselves "Your Imperial Majesty's faithful subjects." They offer the Emperor a summary of their teaching, and they are ready, God willing, to say more from the Scriptures.
documented_stories.title: A Confession Signed by Princes

documented_stories.teaser: At table, Luther said his whole life was patience. A student also remembered a question from his wife, Katharina von Bora. Why did the old church pray so hard, and their own house so coldly?
documented_stories.tellable_as: At his table, Luther told his students that his whole life was patience. He needed it with the Pope, with heretics, with servants, and "with Kate my wife." In another talk, Katharina von Bora is remembered asking why the old church prayed so hard while their own household prayed cold and careless.
documented_stories.telling:
His students wrote down what Luther said one day at table about patience. "I must have patience with the Pope," he told them. He went on to heretics and seducers, to the roaring courtiers, and to his own servants. "I must have patience with Kate my wife; to conclude, the patiences are so many, that my whole life is nothing but patience."

In another conversation, Luther told how his wife had been sick, and how he had prayed for her to recover. He believed God answered that prayer, and gave the household a good farm and a fruitful year besides.

At that time, Katharina herself is remembered asking him a question. "Sir! how is it, that in Popedom they pray so often with great vehemence, but we are very cold and careless in praying?"

Luther answered, as his students recorded it, that the devil drives his own servants on continually. They are diligent in their false worship, "but we, indeed, are ice cold therein, and negligent."
documented_stories.title: Patience and a Question About Prayer
documented_stories.when: Remembered at Luther's table, between 1531 and 1546

floor_note.text: On who Jesus is, this world gives the answer its households said each week. Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. It treats this as received teaching that its own history never had to settle. What it stresses is what he did. He bought back lost people at the cost of his own blood, and he alone stands as their Mediator. Faith in him is trust in a promise.

highlights.note: Archbishop of Mainz and of Magdeburg. Indulgences were being preached under his name, and Luther wrote to him about it in 1517.
Paid letters that cut the penalty for sin. Luther spoke against them in 1517.
Ninety-five points to be debated. Luther sent them to the archbishop with his letter.
Albrecht was archbishop here. The Roman town of Mogontiacum lay on this site, in today's Germany.
The town where Luther taught at the university and wrote his 1517 letter.
The cardinal Luther met at Augsburg in 1518.
Revoco means 'I recant'. Luther said an Italian urged him to say this one word to the cardinal.

An imperial assembly at Worms in 1521. Luther was summoned there, and he was asked whether his books were his.
The city where the Diet met in 1521. Borbetomagus, the ancient place at Worms, lies in today's Germany.
Frederick of Saxony was Luther's prince, and Elector was his title. Luther said Frederick gave him a guard in 1518.
The place where Luther was hidden after Worms, until he returned to Wittenberg in March 1522.
The instruction every Christian needs, the Ten Commandments, the Creed and the Lord's Prayer. Households were told to say them daily.
Forgiveness spoken to a person who has admitted sin, heard as though from God himself. This church kept private confession as a comfort and never forced it.
The meal of bread and wine. This church taught that Christ's body and blood are truly present in and under the bread and wine, and it did not explain how.
The Law terrifies it, and God's promise comforts it.
The scholar who drafted the Augsburg Confession in 1530.

highlights.note: An assembly called by the Emperor in 1530. It met to plan defense against the Turk and to hear the quarrels over religion.
Melanchthon wrote this summary of what the movement taught. Princes and city senates signed it at the Diet of 1530.
The Diet met here in 1530, and Luther met Cajetan here in 1518. The Roman city Augusta Vindelicum stood on this site, in Germany.

Luther's wife. One question of hers is remembered, set down by a student.

legacy.text: This world's own record says that a confessional family grew from these churches. It still teaches a catechism like this world's own and still sings in the language of the people, under many names. This record speaks from the world's own formation, as it was lived. It makes no claim about what those communities believe or practice now.

Three things are not carried forward. This record does not say what came after the prince-and-council church that this world lived under. It closes within a few years of the founder's death, though the confession it holds was gathered by 1580. The tradition went on for centuries beyond that point, in ways not told here. The 1543 treatise is real and part of this world's own history. This record does not say how the churches that came after have answered for it.

read_first.note: The household program in the founder's own words: the three parts, the weekly questions, and the scripts for confession. This edition lacks Luther's 1529 preface. It describes what a household was to do and holds nothing of what any household did.

source.citation: Luther, The Small Catechism (1529), trans. Robert E. Smith, Project Wittenberg (1994/2002/2004)

read_first.note: The founder's own account of why the catechism was needed. It sets out the father's weekly duty to examine his household. His complaint that people held the Gospel lightly is his own word, and no parish report backs it.

source.citation: Luther, The Large Catechism (1529), trans. Bente & Dau, Concordia Triglotta (1921)

read_first.note: This world's own statement of its teaching, signed before the Emperor at Augsburg in 1530 by an elector, princes, and two city senates. It speaks as a shared voice.

source.citation: Melanchthon (drafter), The Augsburg Confession (1530), Project Gutenberg #275

relations_summary.text: This world knew itself partly by what it refused. It refused the claim that authority over doctrine sits with the pope, and it refused the sale of indulgences. Rome answered with a bull in 1520 and a written reply at Augsburg in 1530. It also set limits against the radicals of 1522, and its confession names and condemns the Anabaptists. And it broke with the cities that read the Supper differently, at Marburg in 1529. The Roman side reaches this record only as quoted by the side that answered it.

sourcing.text: This record is richest in the founder's catechisms, treatises, and confessional documents. It is also rich in the movement's own account of its founding decade, 1517 to 1531. It is thinner elsewhere. No parish's own report of receiving this teaching is held. The Saxon visitation records exist but are not in this library. No woman's own text is in this library. The felt experience of the 1529 break at Marburg has not come down to this record. The years after 1531, up to the declared close of 1580, are thin. This library holds no object or outside witness that confirms this world's account of itself. Two real parts of its history are not available to quote: the 1525 tract against the peasants and the 1543 treatise against the Jews.

story.text: From 1517 to 1580, a reform grew out of Wittenberg. Martin Luther taught there at the university.

At the heart of this tradition sits a frightened conscience. The commandments teach a person to despair of his own powers, and then God's promise comforts him. A sinner is freely justified for Christ's sake, through faith. The sacraments carry that promise. Baptism is daily, and absolution is given as though from God himself. In the Supper, Christ's body and blood are truly present, in and under the bread and wine, and this church gives no explanation of how.

On 31 October 1517 Luther, a friar, wrote to Albrecht, the Archbishop of Mainz. Preachers were offering indulgences in the archbishop's name, to help build St. Peter's in Rome. Luther was troubled by what their hearers now believed. He asked the archbishop to withdraw the instruction the preachers worked from. He sent ninety-five statements for debate with it, the Ninety-Five Theses.

In 1518 Luther was summoned to Augsburg. By his own account, told years later at his table, he knelt before Cardinal Cajetan. He would not say the one word an Italian urged on him, Revoco, which means I recant.

In 1521 Luther stood before the Emperor and the Electors at the Diet of Worms. Years afterward he told the story to his students at his own table. By his account, he would not take back his books of teaching. If he had been too violent in his books against opponents, he was willing to be corrected. The next day he would accept instruction in everything except what touches Holy Scripture.

The reform ran ahead of its founder. In March 1522 Luther left the Wartburg, where he had been hidden since Worms, against the Elector's instruction to stay. Wittenberg was in disorder over how fast to sweep away the old forms of worship. Luther preached eight days running and told his congregation he saw no signs of love among them.
On 1 July 1523 two young monks, John and Henry, were burned at Brussels after they refused to give up their teaching. Within months Luther wrote a ballad about them.

The reform also taught people in their own language. German hymns were sung inside the Mass. Wittenberg's first hymn-book was printed in 1524 and held eight hymns, four of them Luther's. Johann Walter later remembered Luther keeping him three weeks at Wittenberg to set the Gospel and Epistle in German, until the first German Mass was sung.

The reform's chief tool for forming people was a household catechism, written in 1529. Its three parts were the Ten Commandments, the Creed and the Lord's Prayer. A father was to question his children and servants at least once a week. The young were to recite the parts daily and get neither food nor drink until they could. After each part came the question, what does this mean? At Luther's own table, a student remembered his wife, Katharina von Bora, asking why the old church prayed with such fervor and their own household so coldly.

In 1530 the Emperor called a Diet to Augsburg, to deal with the Turk and to hear the quarrels over religion. Melanchthon wrote the Augsburg Confession for it. An elector, several princes and the senates of two cities signed it. Luther's name is not among them. The Confession rejected those who taught otherwise about the Supper.
In 1525 Luther wrote against the peasants' rising, and in 1543 he wrote a treatise against the Jews. Scholars disagree about that book's effect in later centuries.

Luther died in the mid-1540s. In 1580 a fuller book of confessions was gathered, the Book of Concord, which drew together the catechisms and the confession given decades before. A family of churches grew from these congregations. They still teach a catechism like this one and still sing in the language of the people.

dates.display: Directly attested in this library's own sources from 31 October 1517 (the letter to Albrecht) to 9 June 1532 (the prayer for rain); no vendored primary text held here gives a birth date. His life is understood to run into 1546, per this world's own already-established closing boundary - a boundary this record treats as given, not independently re-derived from any source of its own.

names.name: Martin Luther (letter to Albrecht of Mainz dated 1517)

voices.hedge: Many stories of Luther here come from students' notes, written down later. The record gives no birth date, no description, and no biography before 1517. His complaints about careless parishes come from him alone. No report from any actual parish backs them.
voices.text: Luther was the friar and Wittenberg professor who wrote to Archbishop Albrecht about indulgences in 1517. He later told his students of facing a papal legate in 1518 and the Empire's assembly at Worms in 1521. In 1522 he came home to calm his own congregation. This record holds him in his own letters, sermons, catechisms, and a ballad. It also holds table talk that students collected. His life closed in the mid-1540s.

dates.display: Documented in this library only as the Augsburg Confession's own drafter, 1530; no vendored source held here gives any other date for him.

names.name: Philip Melanchthon, drafter of the Augsburg Confession (1530)

voices.hedge: This record knows Melanchthon only as the Confession's drafter. It holds no biography, no private letter, and no word of his outside the Confession's shared voice. The record presents the story as a signed act of many people.
voices.text: Melanchthon wrote the Augsburg Confession. It was read to the Emperor in 1530, and princes and city senates signed it. It was a shared statement of what the movement taught.

dates.display: Undated in this library beyond the general span of Luther's own household life as Table Talk records it (a collection compiled mainly in the 1530s-40s, per its own transmission history); no vendored source held here gives her birth or death date, or a date for the one exchange this library records.

voices.hedge: That question is the only place any woman speaks in this record. It passed through several hands, and its exact wording is Contested. This record holds nothing else of her words, her days, or her convictions. It can carry no more than one sentence.
voices.text: Katharina von Bora was Luther's wife. One question of hers survives in this record. She asked why the old church prayed with such fervor while their own household prayed so coldly. A student remembered it and wrote it down years later.

dates.display: Undated in this library beyond his own letter's self-description, written "in his old age," recalling events "some forty years" past; the German Mass work he describes belongs to the mid-1520s (Luther's own effort to establish it), per his own account as quoted in Bacon's Introduction.

names.name: Johann Walter (letter written "in his old age," recalling events of some forty years earlier)

voices.hedge: Walter wrote in his old age, about events some forty years back. His letter reaches this record only as quoted by a later editor, through three earlier hands. It praises Luther throughout, and no second witness confirms it.
voices.text: Johann Walter worked with Luther on the music. He remembered being kept three weeks at Wittenberg while the two of them chose how to sing the Epistle and Gospel in German. His letter is the one account of worship there that does not come from Luther himself.

tile.text: In 1517, Martin Luther, an Augustinian friar and professor at the young university of Wittenberg, wrote to his archbishop against the sale of indulgences. The letter began a movement that set Scripture against a hierarchy standing between people and God. It held that a person stands before God by a gift received through faith, apart from works. Princes and city councils took the reform into their lands in place of bishops. This world's chief tool was the household catechism. It had three parts, to be said at rising, at table, and at night. A father or a schoolmaster was to examine each household every week. The commandments left the conscience afraid, and a promise spoken from outside it made the conscience sure. German hymns were sung inside a Mass that was kept. The story runs from the Ninety-Five Theses to a confession signed before the Emperor at Augsburg in 1530. It closes with a fuller book of confessions, gathered in 1580. The record is rich on the founding decade. It is thin on how any household or parish lived this, and this library holds no woman's own text.
